passages.text: Meera Iyer is head of quality at Arvik Pharma's Baddi plant. During a routine review she finds that a batch of 2 lakh antibiotic strips, shipped to distributors last week, recorded a dissolution result marginally outside the current pharmacopoeia limit. The result would have passed under the older edition of the pharmacopoeia, which the plant's test procedure still quotes in one place. There is no report of patient harm. A recall would cost about ₹3.2 crore and would land in the last week of the quarter, when the CEO has promised investors a margin target. The head of sales suggests a quiet alternative: replace the stock at distributor level during 'routine rotation' over the next six weeks, without informing the regulator. He points out that the regulator is very unlikely to detect the deviation.

Neelgiri Leaf is a packaged-tea brand with a 22% share in Assam and North Bengal. It sells mainly through 9,000 kirana stores, many of which it has supplied on credit for two decades, and its 500 g pack sells at ₹240. Its operating margin is 14%; a ₹40 price cut would wipe that out. A national FMCG company has just launched a competing tea at ₹199, backed by heavy television advertising, and is entering through supermarkets and e-commerce. Neelgiri's strengths are its distributor relationships, the credit it extends to kiranas, a blend tuned to local water and taste, and a loyal older customer base. Its weakness: almost no presence among urban buyers under 30, who account for about 35% of the category's growth.

Rohan Mehta is the top sales manager at a B2B software company and brings in about 30% of his region's revenue. Over two weeks, three junior team members separately tell Farah, the HR head, that Rohan humiliates them in team reviews, mocks their mistakes in group chats and sends demanding messages late at night. One of them says she is preparing to resign. None of them wants to file a formal complaint, fearing retaliation. The regional VP, to whom Rohan reports, tells Farah: 'Rohan's numbers carry this region. Coach him quietly and let's not make this a thing.' The annual promotion cycle closes next month, and Rohan is the front-runner for regional head.

SunGrid, a state-backed power company, plans a 400-acre solar park near Kherwada village in western Rajasthan. Of this, 140 acres is private farmland; owners have been offered 1.5 times the market rate and most have agreed. The remaining 260 acres is government land that about 70 pastoralist households have used for generations as common grazing, without formal title. Because they own no land, the current plan offers them nothing. A local NGO has threatened litigation that could delay the project by two years. The district collector, under pressure to meet a state renewable-energy target, wants work to begin within three months. SunGrid's project return (IRR) is 13% on schedule; a two-year delay would cut it to 9%, below SunGrid's hurdle rate of 11%.

Crumb & Co., a bakery in Indore, has one oven, available for 40 hours a week. It makes three products, each baked in whole batches only:
- Bread: 20 loaves per batch, 1 oven-hour per batch, contribution ₹40 per loaf, weekly demand 400 loaves.
- Cakes: 8 cakes per batch, 2 oven-hours per batch, contribution ₹150 per cake, weekly demand 96 cakes.
- Cookies: 100 cookies per batch, 0.5 oven-hour per batch, contribution ₹6 per cookie, weekly demand 2,000 cookies.
Contribution is selling price minus variable cost. Fixed costs are ₹22,000 a week. Nothing can be sold beyond the stated demand, and the oven is the only constraint on production.

Akshar Trust runs after-school learning centres for 3,000 children in the urban settlements of Hyderabad. Its largest donor will stop funding in six months. A fintech company offers ₹2 crore over three years, about 40% of Akshar's budget, on two conditions: the centres display the company's branding, and the company receives anonymised data from Akshar's household baseline surveys, covering income, spending and borrowing, to 'build credit models that serve underserved families'. When the surveys were done, parents were told the information would be used only to plan Akshar's programmes. The surveys record the locality and lane of each household.

Ganit Pro, a maths-learning app for Classes 9–12, has 4,00,000 free users and 6,000 paid subscribers at ₹2,400 a year. It spends ₹1.1 crore a month more than it earns and has ₹13.2 crore in the bank. The board is weighing two plans. Plan A: put most content behind a paywall; the team expects free users to fall by half but conversion to rise to 4% of the remaining users. Plan B: sell school licences at ₹2 lakh per school per year; the sales team believes 300 private schools could sign, but school sales cycles run six to nine months.

Sundaram Knits, a garment exporter in Tiruppur, employs 800 workers, most of them women who migrated from other districts and live in the company hostel. There is no union. A major European buyer has exited, and orders are down 30%. Mr. Sundaram is considering laying off 240 workers. Talks with a new buyer are under way and could restore orders in about eight months, but nothing is certain. A skilled tailor takes about four months to train to export quality. The mill has enough cash to absorb modest losses for about six months, but not to keep all costs unchanged.

Sahyadri College must transport 600 students daily. Each bus seats 50, and every student must have a seat. Option 1 (Lease): lease rent of ₹60,000 per bus per month, plus ₹40,000 per bus per month for fuel and driver. Option 2 (Contract): a transport company carries students at ₹1,500 per student per month. Option 3 (Buy): buses cost ₹30 lakh each, last 8 years with no resale value, and cost ₹45,000 per bus per month to run (fuel, driver, maintenance). Ignore interest and taxes, and spread the purchase price evenly over the bus's life.

Mrs. Kulkarni is principal of a government-aided school in Pune. Annual Sports Day is scheduled for 10 February, five weeks before the Class 10 board exams. The parents' association has passed a resolution demanding cancellation, saying 'all Class 10 parents' want students to focus on exams. The physical education teacher points out that the district sports office uses Sports Day results, submitted by 28 February, to shortlist students for state-level trials; twelve Class 10 students are in contention. A local sponsor pays ₹3 lakh for the event, money that also buys the school's sports equipment for the year, on condition that it is held in February. Class teachers object that the usual three afternoons of rehearsal eat into revision. Of 180 Class 10 families, 40 are association members, and 25 attended the meeting that passed the resolution.

Rathi Infra is deciding how to bid for a municipal flyover contract. Preparing a bid costs ₹12 lakh, spent whether or not it wins. It can submit only one bid, High or Low.
- High bid: profit of ₹1.5 crore if won; probability of winning 0.3.
- Low bid: profit of ₹80 lakh if won; probability of winning 0.6.
Whichever bid wins, there is a 20% chance that monsoon delays will cut profit by ₹50 lakh. Rathi Infra is short of cash this year. An insurer offers cover for the full ₹50 lakh delay loss for a premium of ₹6 lakh, payable only if Rathi wins and signs the contract.

Bansal Steel Tubes, a ₹400-crore family company in Ludhiana, faces a succession decision. The founder, 68, wants to step back. His son Vikram, 42, has run operations for 15 years; he is cautious and trusted by workers and bankers. His daughter Ananya, 36, a former consultant, joined three years ago and built a solar mounting-structures line that is now 18% of revenue and growing 40% a year. The core tubes business is flat, and margins are falling as cheap imports rise. Vikram says the solar line 'eats plant capacity'. The company's main lender has a covenant: the managing director of the borrowing company must have at least 10 years' experience in the business.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate course of action for Meera?
options: Accept the sales head's plan, since there is no evidence of harm and it avoids a costly recall.
Escalate to the CEO, record her objection in writing, and implement whatever the CEO decides.
Notify the regulator, start a voluntary recall of the batch, and commission a stability study to establish the actual risk.
Retest retained samples of the batch and, if a retest passes, close the deviation.
Wait until the quarter closes and then recall the batch quietly, so that results already promised to investors are protected.
questions.explanation: As quality head, Meera owns batch release. A product outside current specification that is already on the market calls for disclosure and recall whatever the quarter-end pressure, and the stability study tells the firm whether wider action is needed. Escalating to the CEO sounds responsible but hands a regulatory duty to the person under the most commercial pressure while strips keep reaching patients. Retesting until a sample passes is 'testing into compliance', a well-known data-integrity violation.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the sales head's proposal on its own terms?
options: Replacing stock through routine rotation would take about six weeks, by which time most of the batch would already have been sold to patients.
Competitors have carried out voluntary recalls in the past.
The recall cost equals about 4% of the quarter's profit.
The older pharmacopoeia edition is still used in some countries.
Distributors prefer formal recalls for accounting reasons.
questions.explanation: The plan rests on the claim that quiet replacement protects patients as well as a recall does. If most strips are consumed before rotation reaches them, the plan protects nobody and only hides the problem. The distributors' accounting preference is an operational inconvenience and leaves the plan's central premise untouched. The older pharmacopoeia point, if anything, supports the sales head.

questions.stem: The CFO objects to Meera's decision: 'We lose ₹3.2 crore for a deviation that probably harms nobody.' Which response best addresses the CFO?
options: Brand value matters more than ₹3.2 crore, so the cost is irrelevant.
Ethics and money should never be weighed against each other.
Insurance will reimburse most of the recall, so the loss is overstated.

The right comparison is the certain recall cost against the expected cost of concealment (chance of discovery times penalties, licence risk and lost trust), plus patient risk that cannot be priced; and a quality check that bends at quarter-end stops being a check.
The CFO has no say in quality matters and should be told so.
questions.explanation: This option meets the CFO on his own ground, expected value, and adds the costs his framing leaves out, including the damage to the quality system itself. 'Brand value matters more' asserts the conclusion without showing it, so it is a slogan rather than a counter-argument. The insurance claim is unverified and still ignores patient risk.

questions.stem: After the incident, which systemic change would do the most to prevent a repeat?
options: Train the sales team on pharmacopoeia standards so they stop proposing workarounds.
Require the CEO to personally sign off every batch release.
Link quality staff bonuses to on-time shipment so that both functions share targets.
Reduce the number of release tests to lower the chance of borderline results.
Update all specifications and test methods to the current pharmacopoeia, and make batch release report through an independent quality line outside sales and finance.
questions.explanation: The incident had two roots: an outdated specification and commercial pressure near the release decision. This option fixes both. Training the sales team is tempting because it targets the visible actor, but it leaves decision rights unchanged. CEO sign-off places release with the person most exposed to quarter-end pressure, and shipment-linked bonuses make the conflict worse.

questions.stem: What is the most sensible immediate response for Neelgiri Leaf?
options: Cut the price of every pack to ₹199 to defend share before the entrant gains a foothold.
Hold the price of the core pack, strengthen the kirana channel through visibility and service, and launch a small low-priced pack to blunt trial-driven switching.
Shift the entire marketing budget to television to match the entrant's visibility.
Move the brand up-market at ₹400 and abandon the mass segment.
Approach the entrant about selling the company before share starts to fall.
questions.explanation: This plays to Neelgiri's real strengths (distribution, credit and a local blend) and answers the actual threat, cheap trial, without destroying margin. Matching ₹199 is the strongest distractor: a cut of over ₹40 wipes out a 14% margin in a price war against a rival with far deeper pockets. Matching the entrant's television spend fights on the rival's strongest ground.

questions.stem: Neelgiri is considering a separate online-only brand for urban buyers under 30. Which information would be most useful before deciding?
options: The number of television channels on which the entrant advertises.
Whether the entrant makes a profit at ₹199.
Neelgiri's market share ten years ago.
What drives under-30 urban buyers' choice (taste, or convenience and brand image), and what it would cost Neelgiri to acquire such a customer online compared with that customer's lifetime value.
Whether kirana owners like the entrant's sales staff.
questions.explanation: An online brand works only if Neelgiri's advantage, its blend, matters to this segment and if the unit economics hold. The entrant's profitability helps predict how long the ₹199 price will last, but says nothing about whether a youth-focused online brand would succeed. The other options are irrelevant to this specific decision.

questions.stem: Analysts expect the entrant's ₹199 to be a penetration price that will rise after about 18 months. A board member advises: 'Don't cut price; just wait it out.' This advice assumes that:
options: most buyers who switch to the entrant during the 18 months will return once its price rises, that is, the switch does not harden into a habit
the entrant will withdraw from the market after 18 months
Neelgiri's distributors will refuse to stock the entrant
the entrant's tea is of poorer quality
Neelgiri's margins will rise during the 18 months
questions.explanation: Waiting works only if lost customers come back; if tea habits settle within 18 months, waiting hands over the share for good. 'The entrant will withdraw' is stronger than the advice needs, since the advice can work even if the entrant stays, provided its price rises and buyers return. Quality is not required either: buyers might return for price or habit alone.

questions.stem: Kirana owners demand 15 extra days of credit; otherwise, they say, they will give shelf space to the entrant. Neelgiri's working capital is tight. What should it do?
options: Refuse all extra credit, since loyal kiranas will not switch over 15 days.
Grant 15 extra days to all 9,000 stores to remove any reason to switch.
Offer extended credit selectively to high-volume stores in return for display and shelf-share commitments, and fund it through a bank's channel-financing arrangement.
Replace credit with a one-time cash discount to all stores.
Stop supplying any store that stocks the entrant.
questions.explanation: Targeted credit secures shelf space where volume is concentrated, ties the concession to something Neelgiri gets back, and protects tight working capital by using bank finance. Blanket credit is the strongest distractor: across 9,000 stores it is expensive for a cash-tight firm and rewards stores that would not have switched anyway. Cutting off stores that stock the entrant is coercive and pushes them towards the rival.

questions.stem: What should Farah do first?
options: Take no action, since no formal complaint has been filed.
Confront Rohan immediately, name the juniors who complained, and warn him.
Follow the VP's advice: coach Rohan quietly and let the promotion go ahead.

Run a confidential, structured fact-finding (speak to the three juniors and others in the team, review the group messages), assure everyone of non-retaliation, and tell the promotion committee that a review is pending.
Transfer the three juniors to another manager to remove the friction.
questions.explanation: Facts must be established before a decision as consequential as a promotion, and the complainants need protection. Coaching may well be part of the outcome, but promoting Rohan before the facts are known rewards the behaviour and gives him more power over the people who complained. Naming the juniors breaches confidentiality and invites the retaliation they fear.

questions.stem: Suppose the inquiry confirms the juniors' accounts. What is the most appropriate decision?
options: Promote Rohan anyway; management style is secondary to results in sales.
Defer the promotion, issue a documented warning with a coaching plan, and make any future promotion conditional on better 360-degree feedback and team retention.
Dismiss Rohan immediately to signal zero tolerance.
Promote Rohan but move the three juniors out of his reporting line.
Leave the decision to the regional VP, since Rohan reports to him.
questions.explanation: The response is proportionate: it signals clearly that leadership roles require people outcomes while giving a high performer a fair chance to change. Immediate dismissal is the strongest distractor. Public humiliation and after-hours pressure are serious, but as a first documented finding (with no sexual or discriminatory element) they call for progressive discipline, not dismissal. Promoting him while moving the victims rewards the conduct.

questions.stem: The regional VP's stance is best described as:
options: a sound utilitarian judgement, since Rohan's revenue benefits more people than the juniors' discomfort harms
reasonable, because informal complaints carry no weight
a legitimate handing-over of people issues to HR
correct, because sales teams need tough managers
a short-term trade-off that ignores the hidden costs of attrition and signals that high performers are exempt from conduct norms
questions.explanation: The VP counts Rohan's revenue but not the cost of resignations, replacement hiring, damaged morale, or the precedent that results excuse behaviour. The utilitarian option is the trap: a genuine utilitarian count would include all of those costs, which the VP leaves out. The VP is also not handing the issue to HR; he is telling HR to drop it.

questions.stem: Which evidence would most strengthen Farah's case, to a numbers-driven VP, that Rohan's behaviour is a business problem?
options: Attrition and exit-interview themes in Rohan's team compared with other teams, plus the cost of hiring and ramping up a replacement sales rep.
Rohan's year-on-year revenue growth.
Industry surveys on the effect of management style on productivity.
The number of hours Rohan works each week.
Whether competitors have managers like Rohan.
questions.explanation: To persuade a VP who thinks in numbers, translate the behaviour into its cost in his own team. Industry surveys are relevant but generic: they do not show that the problem exists here or what it costs. Rohan's revenue growth supports the VP's side, not Farah's.

questions.stem: What is the best course of action for SunGrid?
options: Proceed on schedule, since the 260 acres is government land and no compensation is legally owed to the grazers.
File a caveat in court to pre-empt the NGO's litigation and proceed.

Negotiate with the grazing households: keep grazing corridors and allow controlled grazing under raised panels, offer jobs in panel cleaning and security, and set up a community fund, recognising customary use even without title.
Move the project to another state where there are no grazing claims.
Pay each family a one-time cash amount per head of livestock and proceed.
questions.explanation: This answers the grazers' real interest, a continuing livelihood, and avoids a two-year delay that would push the IRR below the hurdle. So it is both the fair choice and the commercially sound one. 'Proceed because it is government land' is the strongest distractor: legal title does not remove the litigation risk or the legitimacy problem, and the delay it invites destroys the project's economics. A one-time cash payment leaves families with no livelihood once the money is spent and can divide the community.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the NGO's position?
options: The private landowners received a premium of 1.5 times the market rate.
The state's renewable-energy target is behind schedule.
Solar panels lower ground temperature beneath them.
Revenue records classify the 260 acres as designated village grazing land, whose diversion legally requires the consent of the village assembly.
The NGO has won similar cases in other districts.
questions.explanation: This turns a moral claim into a legal one: if diversion needs village consent, the project cannot proceed without engaging the grazers. The NGO's past wins elsewhere suggest a credible threat but say nothing about the merits of this case. The premium paid to landowners concerns a different group.

questions.stem: The collector suggests a faster route: begin fencing the land under police protection. What is the most serious risk of this approach?
options: Fencing costs may rise because of the police deployment.
A confrontation could lead to a court injunction and reputational damage that lenders with environmental and social safeguards would treat as a red flag, endangering this and future projects.
The state target might be met too early.
The private landowners might demand more money.
Police deployment would require extra paperwork.
questions.explanation: Force invites exactly the delay SunGrid cannot afford, and it can damage its access to finance for every later project. The landowners demanding more is possible but minor next to an injunction and a financing red flag. The cost and paperwork options are trivial in comparison.

questions.stem: The collector argues: 'Most landowners have agreed, so the village clearly supports the project.' What is the main flaw in this argument?
options: The landowners were paid a premium, so their consent was bought.
The village may change its mind later.
Not every landowner agreed.
The collector is under pressure to meet a target.
Consent from landowners cannot speak for the landless grazers, whose interests are different; the group consulted does not represent everyone affected.
questions.explanation: The argument generalises from one group (owners, who are being paid) to the whole village, including the people who lose most and are offered nothing. 'Consent was bought' is tempting but wrong: paying a premium does not invalidate consent. Pointing to the collector's pressure attacks his motive rather than his reasoning.

questions.stem: To maximise weekly contribution, how many cakes should Crumb & Co. bake?
questions.explanation: The oven is the bottleneck, so rank products by contribution per oven-hour: cookies ₹1,200 (100 × 6 ÷ 0.5), bread ₹800 (20 × 40 ÷ 1), cakes ₹600 (8 × 150 ÷ 2). Cookies (10 h) and bread (20 h) meet full demand in 30 h, and the remaining 10 h make 5 cake batches, or 40 cakes. 96 is the trap from ranking by contribution per unit, where cakes look best at ₹150 each.

questions.stem: What is the maximum weekly profit?
questions.explanation: Contribution = 2,000 × 6 + 400 × 40 + 40 × 150 = 12,000 + 16,000 + 6,000 = ₹34,000; less fixed costs of ₹22,000 gives ₹12,000. ₹34,000 is contribution before fixed costs. ₹5,200 is what the per-unit ranking produces: 96 cakes (24 h, ₹14,400) plus 320 loaves (16 h, ₹12,800) = ₹27,200, minus ₹22,000.

questions.stem: A café offers to buy 800 extra cookies a week, over and above regular demand, at a price that gives a contribution of only ₹4.50 per cookie. Should Crumb & Co. accept, and what happens to weekly profit?
options: Reject: ₹4.50 is below the regular contribution of ₹6.
Accept: profit rises by ₹3,600.
Accept: profit rises by ₹400.
Accept: profit rises by ₹1,200.
Reject: profit falls by ₹1,200.
questions.explanation: 800 cookies = 8 batches = 4 oven-hours. The oven is already full, so those hours come from the lowest-value use, cakes: 2 batches = 16 cakes × ₹150 = ₹2,400 forgone. The gain is 800 × 4.50 = ₹3,600, so profit rises by ₹1,200 (the order earns ₹900 per oven-hour against cakes' ₹600). ₹3,600 ignores the opportunity cost, and ₹400 wrongly assumes bread would be displaced.

questions.stem: Ignoring the café order, the owner can rent a second small oven that adds 8 oven-hours a week for ₹4,000 a week. What should she do?
options: Rent: profit rises by ₹5,600.
Rent: profit rises by ₹800.
Do not rent: profit falls by ₹800.
Rent: profit rises by ₹2,400.
Do not rent: the extra hours add no saleable output.
questions.explanation: Cookie and bread demand is already met, so the extra 8 hours go to cakes: 4 batches = 32 cakes (72 in total, within demand of 96), worth 32 × 150 = ₹4,800. Less ₹4,000 rent, profit rises by ₹800. ₹5,600 assumes the hours earn the cookie rate of ₹1,200 per hour, which is impossible because cookie demand is already satisfied.

questions.stem: With the original single oven, and ignoring the café order and the second oven, by how much would weekly profit rise if two more oven-hours became available?
options: Nothing, because demand is the binding limit
questions.explanation: Extra hours go to the only product still short of demand, cakes: 2 hours = 1 batch = 8 cakes × ₹150 = ₹1,200. This is the 'shadow price' of the bottleneck, ₹600 per hour. ₹2,400 applies the cookie rate, but cookie demand is already met. The last option is wrong because cakes are still 56 short of demand.

questions.stem: What is the best response for Akshar Trust?
options: Accept the funding with branding, but share no household data unless families give fresh, informed, opt-in consent for that specific use; offer aggregated, non-identifiable insights instead.
Accept both conditions, since the data is anonymised and the money keeps centres open.
Reject the offer outright, because corporate money compromises an NGO.
Accept both conditions and inform parents afterwards through a notice at the centres.
Accept the data condition but refuse the branding, since branding commercialises children's spaces.
questions.explanation: This keeps the money while honouring the purpose for which the data was collected. Accepting both conditions is the strongest distractor: anonymisation does not cure consent given for a different purpose, and household data tagged by lane can often be re-identified. The last option has the priorities backwards, since branding is a minor issue and data use is the serious breach.

questions.stem: The fintech says: 'The data is anonymised, so there is no privacy issue.' What is the strongest reason this does not settle the matter?
options: Anonymised data is always useless for building models.
The fintech company may go bankrupt.
Akshar's data-storage costs would rise.
Consent was given for programme planning only, and detailed household data tied to small localities can often be re-identified and later used to deny or price credit for the same families.
Parents cannot understand what anonymisation means.
questions.explanation: It combines both problems: the use falls outside the purpose parents agreed to, and the protection is weaker than claimed for lane-level data. 'Parents cannot understand anonymisation' is condescending and misses the point; the issue is that parents were never asked. The first option is plainly false.

questions.stem: A board member argues: 'Without this money, 1,200 children lose their classes. Worrying about abstract data rights is a luxury we can't afford.' What is the most effective counter?
options: Education matters more than privacy, so the board member is right.

The choice is not either-or: accepting with branding only, or bridge funding, may close the gap, and breaking parents' trust could empty the centres, harming the very children the money is meant to serve.
Educating children is the government's job, not Akshar's.
Data rights are protected by law, so the argument is irrelevant.
The fintech should be asked to double its grant.
questions.explanation: The board member's argument is a false dilemma, and this answer exposes it while also showing that the breach would hurt the children through lost trust. The appeal to law asserts a conclusion without engaging the funding problem; even if the law applies, the gap remains. Agreeing with the board member accepts the false dilemma.

questions.stem: The fintech's claim that the data will 'serve underserved families' depends most on which assumption?
options: Underserved families currently have no access to credit of any kind.
Akshar's surveys are accurate.
The fintech will make a profit.
Families want to borrow more money.
Better credit models will bring these families more or cheaper credit, rather than more precise exclusion or higher prices for those judged risky.
questions.explanation: Better models only 'serve' families if they are used to include them; the same model can sharpen exclusion. That gap between 'better model' and 'better outcome' is the hidden assumption. Survey accuracy is needed for the model to work at all, but even an accurate model can harm, so accuracy is not the link the 'serve' claim rests on. 'No access of any kind' is stronger than the claim needs.

questions.stem: If Plan A works as projected, by how much does annual subscription revenue change?
options: +₹1.92 crore
+₹2.4 crore
+₹48 lakh
−₹24 lakh
+₹24 lakh
questions.explanation: Current revenue: 6,000 × ₹2,400 = ₹1.44 crore. Plan A: 4,00,000 ÷ 2 = 2,00,000 users × 4% = 8,000 subscribers × ₹2,400 = ₹1.92 crore. The change is +₹48 lakh. ₹1.92 crore is the new total, not the change, and ₹2.4 crore forgets that free users halve (16,000 × 2,400 − 1.44 crore).

questions.stem: Which conclusion follows most directly from the figures?
options: Plan A should be adopted because it raises revenue immediately.
Plan B will make the company profitable within a year.
The company should shut down.
Plan A will extend the runway by about six months.
Plan A adds only about ₹4 lakh a month against a ₹1.1 crore monthly burn, so neither revenue plan alone fixes the runway; cost cuts or fresh funding are needed whichever plan is chosen.
questions.explanation: The ₹48 lakh a year is about ₹4 lakh a month, under 4% of the burn. The runway is ₹13.2 crore ÷ ₹1.1 crore = 12 months, so the real problem is cost and funding. 'Six more months of runway' is the trap: ₹13.2 crore ÷ ₹1.06 crore is about 12.5 months, an extension of roughly two weeks.

questions.stem: What is the most serious risk in relying on Plan B?
options: Schools might prefer a cheaper competitor.
Even if schools sign, a six-to-nine-month sales cycle means cash arrives when only three to six months of runway remain, so the plan depends on bridge funding or cost cuts in the meantime.
Students may not use the app in school.
₹2 lakh is too low a price for schools.
Teachers may resist technology.
questions.explanation: This risk is specific and existential: it sets the timing of cash against a 12-month runway. Competition from cheaper rivals is real but generic, and would apply to any plan. Classroom usage and teacher resistance affect renewals more than survival.

questions.stem: What is the most prudent next step for the board?
options: Roll out Plan A to all users next month.
Commit to Plan B and hire 20 salespeople.
Hire a consultancy to study the edtech market for three months.
Run a paywall test on a random slice of users and a paid pilot with a few schools in parallel, while cutting non-essential costs to stretch the runway.
Make the app entirely free to maximise users before the next funding round.
questions.explanation: This buys evidence on both plans cheaply and quickly while protecting the runway. Going fully free is the strongest distractor, because user growth can help fundraising, but with 12 months of cash and no revenue plan it bets everything on investors' appetite. A three-month study burns a quarter of the runway without testing anything.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate course of action for Mr. Sundaram?
options: Lay off the 240 most recently hired workers immediately to restore margins.
Impose a uniform 20% pay cut on everyone for six months.

Combine a shorter working week with graded pay reductions (largest for management and higher earners, smallest for the lowest-paid), explain the situation openly, and review monthly as talks with the new buyer progress.
Keep full pay and full staff, financing all losses from the mill's cash until orders return.
Shut the mill temporarily and rehire when orders return.
questions.explanation: This keeps the trained workforce for the likely recovery, spreads the burden according to ability to bear it, and stays within the cash available. The uniform 20% cut is the strongest distractor: it sounds equal but takes the same share from workers near subsistence as from managers, and it is not linked to reduced hours. Keeping everything unchanged exceeds what the mill's cash can absorb.

questions.stem: Which consideration most strongly argues against layoffs in this case?
options: Recovery is possible in about eight months and a skilled tailor takes four months to train, so rehiring and retraining after layoffs could cost more than retaining workers through the dip.
The workers are migrants with nowhere else to go.
There is no union to negotiate with.
Layoffs are illegal in the textile industry.
Layoffs would make the owner unpopular in Tiruppur.
questions.explanation: This is a hard business argument built from the facts in the case: the cost and time of rebuilding skill against a likely recovery. The workers' vulnerability is a strong moral consideration, but it is not the most decisive argument here, and it does not engage the economics. The legality claim is false.

questions.stem: If some job losses became unavoidable, which method of selecting workers is most defensible?
options: Supervisors choose based on their own judgement of attitude.
Last in, first out, applied mechanically.
Remove those who complained most often about working conditions.
Select workers from one hostel block to simplify logistics.
First offer voluntary separation with severance; then apply pre-announced criteria combining skill needs and length of service, with priority recall when orders return.
questions.explanation: This option is voluntary first, then transparent, skill-aware and reversible through recall. Mechanical last-in-first-out is objective, which makes it the strongest distractor, but it ignores skills and may remove tailors the mill needs to win the new buyer. Choosing those who complained is retaliation, and supervisor judgement invites bias.

questions.stem: Mr. Sundaram wants to keep the new-buyer talks secret from workers 'to avoid false hope'. Which evaluation is most sound?
options: Right: sharing uncertain news is always irresponsible.
Right: workers have no stake in commercial negotiations.
Wrong: the owner must share all contract details with workers.
Wrong: a candid, qualified update ('talks are on, nothing is certain') helps retain skilled workers who might otherwise leave and builds trust for the sacrifices being asked of them.
Irrelevant: workers will hear about it anyway.
questions.explanation: Workers are being asked to accept cuts, and an honest reason to stay reduces the loss of exactly the people the mill needs. 'Share all contract details' goes too far: commercial terms can legitimately stay confidential, and what matters is that talks exist and how far they have got. 'Always irresponsible' is an absolute claim that does not hold.

questions.stem: For 600 students, which option is cheapest per month?
options: Contract, at ₹9,00,000
Lease and Buy cost the same
questions.explanation: 600 ÷ 50 = 12 buses. Lease: 12 × ₹1,00,000 = ₹12,00,000. Contract: 600 × ₹1,500 = ₹9,00,000. Buy: ₹30,00,000 ÷ 96 months = ₹31,250 + ₹45,000 = ₹76,250 per bus × 12 = ₹9,15,000. The contract is cheapest by ₹15,000. ₹5,40,000 counts only running costs (12 × 45,000) and ignores the purchase price.

questions.stem: The transport company raises its rate by 4%. For 600 students, which option is now cheapest, and by how much per month over the next cheapest?
options: Contract, by ₹21,000
Contract, by ₹6,000
questions.explanation: New rate: ₹1,500 × 1.04 = ₹1,560; 600 × 1,560 = ₹9,36,000. Buying costs ₹9,15,000, so it is cheaper by ₹21,000. ₹36,000 is the size of the price rise itself (9,36,000 − 9,00,000), not the gap between the options.

questions.stem: At the original contract rate, enrolment rises to 640 students. Which option is cheaper per month between Buy and Contract, and by how much?
options: Contract, by ₹16,000
They cost the same
Contract, by ₹31,250
questions.explanation: 640 ÷ 50 = 12.8, so 13 buses are needed, because a bus cannot be bought in fractions. Buy: 13 × ₹76,250 = ₹9,91,250. Contract: 640 × ₹1,500 = ₹9,60,000. The contract is cheaper by ₹31,250. 'Contract by ₹16,000' comes from using 12.8 buses (₹9,76,000), ignoring that the 13th bus runs mostly empty.

questions.stem: For 600 students, what minimum percentage discount on the lease rent alone (fuel and driver unchanged) would make leasing cost the same as the contract at ₹1,500?
questions.explanation: To match ₹9,00,000 with 12 buses, each bus may cost ₹75,000. Fuel and driver stay at ₹40,000, so the lease rent must fall to ₹35,000, a cut of ₹25,000 on ₹60,000, or 41.7%. 58.3% is ₹35,000 ÷ ₹60,000, the rent that remains, mistaken for the discount.

questions.stem: The principal prefers buying because 'at least we will own an asset'. What is the strongest objection?
options: The buses have no resale value and lock the college into an eight-year commitment that already costs slightly more than contracting, and costs clearly more whenever enrolment does not fill whole buses.
Owned buses cannot be insured.
Contractors are always safer than in-house drivers.
Owning assets is never good for an educational institution.
Buying requires more buses than leasing.
questions.explanation: With zero resale value, 'owning an asset' adds nothing at the end; the college pays more and loses flexibility, as the 640-student case shows. 'Owning assets is never good' is an overgeneralisation with no support in the case. Buying needs the same 12 buses as leasing, so the last option is false.

questions.stem: What is the best decision for Mrs. Kulkarni?
options: Cancel Sports Day this year; board exams come first.

Hold a compressed one-day event in February with rehearsals outside class hours, make Class 10 participation optional except for students competing for state trials, and submit results by the deadline.
Hold Sports Day exactly as planned; traditions should not bend to pressure.
Postpone Sports Day to June, after the exams.
Let the sponsor decide the format, since it pays for the event.
questions.explanation: This meets every core interest: revision time is protected, the twelve students keep their trial chance, and the sponsor money for the whole school's equipment is kept. Postponing to June is the strongest distractor: it removes exam pressure but misses the 28 February deadline and loses the February-conditional sponsorship. Cancelling hurts the same students in the same way.

questions.stem: What do the attendance figures suggest about the association's claim to speak for 'all Class 10 parents'?
options: A majority of Class 10 parents want cancellation.
Most Class 10 parents support Sports Day.
The resolution reflects the 25 of 180 families (about 14%) who chose to attend; it cannot be read as the view of all Class 10 parents, and a quick survey of every family would be more reliable.
The association should be dissolved for misrepresentation.
The 140 non-member families agree with the association.
questions.explanation: 25 ÷ 180 ≈ 13.9%, a small, self-selected group, so the claim is unrepresentative. 'Most parents support Sports Day' over-reaches in the other direction: silence is not support either, and the data only show that the claim is unproven. Nothing supports the first or last options.

questions.stem: The sponsor now asks that last year's Class 10 toppers appear in its advertisements as a condition of renewing next year. What should the principal do?
options: Agree, since the toppers' families would probably consent.
Agree, but only after this year's exams are over.
Refuse and end the sponsorship.
Let the toppers decide for themselves.
Decline to use students in advertising and offer the sponsor other visibility, such as banners, a named trophy and a mention in the school magazine.
questions.explanation: A school should not turn minors' academic results into brand advertising, but the sponsor's legitimate interest, visibility, can be met in other ways. 'Agree after exams' is the strongest distractor: it fixes the timing but not the principle, and consent obtained under the school's influence is not freely given. Ending the sponsorship throws away a negotiable relationship.

questions.stem: Which principle best explains the recommended approach to this dispute?
options: Focus on each party's underlying interests (revision time, trial selection, funding) rather than on their stated positions of 'cancel' or 'hold as is'.
The majority view should always prevail.
The party paying the money decides.
Tradition should take precedence over short-term concerns.
The principal should avoid any decision that upsets a group.
questions.explanation: This is interest-based negotiation: positions conflict, but the interests behind them can often all be met. Majority rule is the strongest distractor, but the 'majority' here is unproven, and majority rule can override a minority with a deadline-bound stake, the twelve students. Avoiding upsetting anyone leads to no decision at all.

questions.stem: Without insurance, which bid has the higher expected value, and by how much?
options: High bid, by ₹12 lakh
Low bid, by ₹3 lakh
Low bid, by ₹6 lakh
Both give the same expected value, ₹30 lakh
High bid, by ₹3 lakh
questions.explanation: High: expected profit if won = 150 − 0.2 × 50 = ₹140 lakh; 0.3 × 140 = 42; less the ₹12 lakh bid cost = ₹30 lakh. Low: 80 − 10 = 70; 0.6 × 70 = 42; less 12 = ₹30 lakh. They are equal. 'Low by ₹3 lakh' is what you get if you ignore the monsoon risk (High 45 − 12 = 33, Low 48 − 12 = 36).

questions.stem: Given that Rathi Infra is short of cash, which bid should it prefer without insurance?
options: High bid, because its profit when it wins is almost double.
Low bid, because with equal expected value it wins twice as often, cutting the chance of losing the ₹12 lakh bid cost from 70% to 40%.
High bid, because the probability of a monsoon delay is lower.
Either bid, since the expected values are equal and risk does not matter.
Neither, since both carry some chance of losing money.
questions.explanation: When expected values tie, a firm that cannot absorb a loss should choose the option with less downside risk. 'Either bid' is the strongest distractor: equal expected value does not make options equivalent for a cash-strapped firm, because variance and the chance of loss matter. The delay probability is the same for both bids, and refusing to bid gives up a positive expected value.

questions.stem: A rival withdraws, raising the High bid's winning probability to 0.4; the Low bid's stays at 0.6. Without insurance, by how much does the High bid's expected value now exceed the Low bid's?
options: ₹6 lakh
₹12 lakh
₹18 lakh
₹4 lakh
₹14 lakh
questions.explanation: High: 0.4 × 140 − 12 = 56 − 12 = ₹44 lakh. Low is unchanged at ₹30 lakh. The difference is ₹14 lakh. ₹18 lakh comes from ignoring the monsoon risk on the High bid only (0.4 × 150 − 12 = 48, minus 30).

questions.stem: Under the original probabilities, Rathi bids Low and buys the delay cover. What is its expected value?
options: ₹26.4 lakh
₹30 lakh
₹32.4 lakh
₹36 lakh
₹42 lakh
questions.explanation: With cover, the delay loss disappears, but the ₹6 lakh premium is paid if Rathi wins: profit if won = 80 − 6 = ₹74 lakh; 0.6 × 74 = 44.4; less 12 = ₹32.4 lakh. Cover is worth buying because the premium (₹6 lakh) is below the expected delay loss (0.2 × 50 = ₹10 lakh). ₹30 lakh results from charging the premium even when Rathi loses; ₹26.4 lakh double-counts by paying the premium and still bearing the delay.

questions.stem: Which succession structure is most appropriate?
options: Make Vikram MD of the whole company, with Ananya reporting to him.
Make Ananya MD of the whole company, since her business is the growth engine.

Place the solar business in a separate subsidiary led by Ananya with its own capital plan, keep Vikram as MD of the core tubes company, and set up a board with independent directors and a family council, with the founder as chairman for a fixed transition period.
Bring in a professional CEO above both siblings immediately.
Sell the solar business to fund modernisation of the tubes plant.
questions.explanation: This matches each sibling to the business they have proven they can run, gives the fast-growing line room and capital, and builds governance to settle future disputes. A professional CEO is the strongest distractor: it can work, but putting an outsider over two capable siblings before governance and capital allocation are settled leaves the core conflict unresolved. Making Vikram MD of everything subordinates the growth line to a cautious operator who already resents it.

questions.stem: Which information is most relevant for deciding how to allocate capital between the two businesses?
options: Each sibling's personal preference.
The return on capital employed, growth outlook and capital needs of each business, together with the threat imports pose to the tubes business.
The founder's original vision for the company.
Which business employs more workers.
Which sibling has the stronger educational qualifications.
questions.explanation: Capital should follow returns, growth and strategic risk. Employment numbers matter socially and must be managed in any transition, but they are a constraint, not the basis for allocating capital. The other options concern people rather than the economics of the businesses.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens Vikram's claim that the solar line 'eats plant capacity'?
options: The solar structures are made on capacity that was lying idle because tube demand had fallen.
Solar structures earn higher margins than tubes.
Ananya has hired her own sales team.
Solar demand is growing nationally.
Some tube customers have also bought solar structures.
questions.explanation: If the solar line uses idle capacity, the tubes business gives up nothing, so there is no cannibalisation. Higher solar margins are the strongest distractor: they might justify the trade-off, but they concede that capacity is being diverted rather than denying it. National growth and the sales team are irrelevant to capacity.

questions.stem: What follows from the lender's covenant?
options: Ananya cannot hold any leadership role in the group.
The company must change its lender.
A professional CEO must be hired.
Unless the covenant is renegotiated, the MD of the borrowing company must be Vikram or someone else with 10 or more years in the business; Ananya could lead a separately structured subsidiary.
The founder must remain MD indefinitely.
questions.explanation: The covenant restricts only who can be MD of the borrowing entity. Vikram (15 years) qualifies and Ananya (3 years) does not, which fits the subsidiary structure. 'The founder must remain MD' is the strongest distractor: he qualifies, but nothing forces him to stay, since he is one option, not a necessity. 'Ananya cannot lead anything' overstates the covenant.

questions.stem: Kabir, a first-year auditor, is asked by his senior, Neha, to sign the inventory-count sheet as a witness to a warehouse count he did not attend. Neha says she did the count herself, the client has been with the firm for years, and the signature is 'a formality'. The audit deadline is tomorrow. What should Kabir do?
options: Sign, since Neha takes responsibility as the senior.
Decline to sign as a witness to something he did not observe, offer to do a quick test count of a sample of items before the deadline, and escalate to the manager if pressed.
Sign, but keep a private note recording that he was not present.
Refuse, and report Neha to the firm's ethics committee immediately.
Ask the client's storekeeper to sign in his place.
questions.explanation: A witness signature asserts something Kabir did not see; declining it while offering a practical fix respects both integrity and the deadline. A private note is the strongest distractor: the official record would still be false, and the note only protects Kabir. Going straight to the ethics committee skips a reasonable fix and the normal escalation path.

questions.stem: Lata heads procurement at a hospital chain and sits on the panel that will decide next month whether to renew a ₹40-crore equipment contract with MedAxis. MedAxis runs a free coding bootcamp, worth about ₹1.5 lakh, for 'children of partner organisations', with seats allotted by lottery. Lata's son has won a seat in what appears to be a fair lottery. What should Lata do?
options: Accept the seat; the lottery was fair, so there is no conflict.
Decline the seat quietly and tell no one.
Accept the seat and vote against MedAxis to prove her neutrality.
Ask MedAxis to hold the seat until after the renewal decision.
Disclose the benefit to the hospital's compliance team and step aside from the MedAxis evaluation, letting compliance decide whether the seat may be kept.
questions.explanation: A fair lottery does not remove the appearance of a conflict; disclosure and recusal protect both the decision and Lata. Declining quietly is the strongest distractor: it removes the benefit but hides from the organisation a relationship it should know about, and disclosure is the core duty. Deferring the seat until after the decision looks like a reward timed to the vote.

questions.stem: Team lead Sameer must pick one person for a six-month overseas client project. Priya has the stronger performance record and returned from maternity leave two months ago; when asked, she said she wants the assignment and has arranged childcare. Arjun is rated slightly lower and has no constraints. Sameer's manager suggests Arjun, 'since Priya has a baby and it's kinder not to burden her'. What should Sameer do?
options: Offer the project to Priya on merit and her stated availability, and agree check-ins and reasonable flexibility as he would for anyone.
Choose Arjun, as the manager suggests, to avoid putting pressure on Priya.
Ask HR to decide so that he avoids a conflict with his manager.
Split the project between Priya and Arjun for three months each.
Choose Arjun but give Priya a bonus to compensate.
questions.explanation: Priya is the stronger candidate and has stated her choice as an adult; respecting it is both fair and good for the client. Choosing Arjun 'out of kindness' is the strongest distractor: overriding someone's stated choice because of parenthood is benevolent bias and, in effect, discrimination. Splitting the project harms continuity with the client just to avoid a decision.

questions.stem: Divya takes over a team in an insurance back office. Mr. Pillai, 55, with 25 years of service and a good record, has been making frequent errors since new claims software arrived six months ago. Two younger colleagues quietly fix his errors. What should Divya do first?
options: Put him on a formal performance-improvement plan with a 30-day deadline.
Suggest he consider voluntary retirement.
Move him to filing work where the software is not used.
Meet him privately to understand the difficulty, arrange focused hands-on training with clear, measurable milestones, and stop the informal error-fixing so that his real progress can be seen.
Ask the two colleagues to keep fixing his errors so that output stays steady.
questions.explanation: The evidence points to a skill gap with new software, not a lack of willingness or ability, so the first step is diagnosis and training with measurable milestones. Moving him to filing is the strongest distractor: it looks kind but writes off an experienced employee without trying the obvious fix, and can read as age-based sidelining. A 30-day formal plan disciplines a training problem.

questions.stem: The municipal commissioner of a mid-sized city receives three sets of complaints about a crowded market street: shopkeepers say street vendors block their storefronts; pedestrians say they are forced onto the road; and about 150 registered vendors say this street is their only livelihood. Which plan best balances these interests?
options: Remove all vendors from the street to clear the footpath.
Allow vendors to operate anywhere, since their livelihood matters most.

Mark numbered vending spaces in the wider stretches and an adjacent lane, keep a clear walking strip, license the registered vendors, and set up a committee of vendor, shopkeeper and resident representatives to resolve disputes.
Auction vending spaces to the highest bidders to raise municipal revenue.
Ask shopkeepers to employ the vendors.
questions.explanation: This gives each group something it needs (space for vendors, access for shops, a walkway for pedestrians) and creates a forum for future disputes. The auction is the strongest distractor: it allocates space 'efficiently' on paper but prices out the poorest registered vendors, failing one group entirely. Removing all vendors or allowing them anywhere each serves one side only.

questions.stem: A 120-flat housing society in Bengaluru must decide on EV charging. Twelve residents own EVs and want basement chargers. Upgrading the building's main electrical supply, needed for any chargers, costs ₹9 lakh; each charger costs ₹60,000. Several non-EV owners object to paying anything. Which cost-sharing approach is most defensible?
options: All 120 flats share the full cost equally, since chargers are a common facility.

Each EV owner pays for their own charger and metered electricity; the supply upgrade, which also adds capacity and value to the whole building, comes from the common fund, possibly with EV owners paying a larger share.
EV owners pay the entire ₹9 lakh upgrade plus their own chargers.
Postpone the decision until most flats own EVs.
Ban EV charging in the building on safety grounds.
questions.explanation: Private benefits (chargers, electricity) fall on users, while the shared, value-adding upgrade is shared, which is the benefit principle applied fairly. Making EV owners pay for everything is the strongest distractor: it loads a building-wide improvement onto 12 flats and could stall adoption altogether. Equal sharing of everything makes non-users fund private chargers.

questions.stem: SkyLink, a low-cost airline, is considering a new route on which a single full-service carrier charges high fares and flies half-empty planes. SkyLink expects the incumbent to cut fares sharply if it enters. Which information matters MOST to SkyLink's decision?
options: The incumbent's reputation among business travellers.
The number of airports in the region.
Fares on the route five years ago.
SkyLink's own advertising budget.
How the incumbent's cost per seat compares with SkyLink's, and how long the incumbent can sustain lower fares on this route.
questions.explanation: If a price war is expected, the winner is whoever has lower costs and can hold out longer, so relative cost and staying power decide the entry. The incumbent's brand among business travellers matters for which customers SkyLink can win, but not whether it survives the fare war. Past fares and SkyLink's own advertising budget are secondary.

questions.stem: A hospital canteen sells 500 meals a day at ₹80 each; the variable cost is ₹50 per meal. The manager proposes a 10% price cut. By what minimum percentage must daily volume rise so that total daily contribution does not fall?
questions.explanation: Current contribution = 500 × (80 − 50) = ₹15,000. New price ₹72 gives ₹22 per meal; the volume needed is 15,000 ÷ 22 ≈ 681.8 meals, a rise of about 36.4%. 11.1% (1 ÷ 0.9 − 1) would keep revenue constant, but the whole ₹8 cut comes out of a ₹30 margin, so volume must rise far more.

questions.stem: Vardhan Motors makes 2,000 units a month of a component at a variable cost of ₹140 per unit. Factory overhead allocated to it is ₹60 per unit and would continue if production stopped. A supplier offers the component at ₹170. If Vardhan buys, the freed machine time could make another product earning ₹45,000 a month in contribution. What should Vardhan do?
options: Keep making the component; it is ₹15,000 a month cheaper.
Buy; it saves ₹60,000 a month.
Buy; it saves ₹1,05,000 a month.
Keep making; it saves ₹60,000 a month.
Buy; it saves ₹15,000 a month.
questions.explanation: Relevant cost to make = 2,000 × ₹140 = ₹2,80,000. Buying costs 2,000 × ₹170 = ₹3,40,000 but frees capacity worth ₹45,000, a net ₹2,95,000. Making is cheaper by ₹15,000. 'Buy saves ₹60,000' compares ₹170 with the full cost of ₹200, but the ₹60 overhead continues either way, so it is irrelevant.

questions.stem: A firm scores three vendors out of 10, weighting price 40%, quality 35% and delivery 25%. Vendor P: price 8, quality 6, delivery 7. Vendor Q: 6, 9, 6. Vendor R: 7, 7, 8. Management then changes the weights to price 40%, quality 45% and delivery 15%. Which vendor ranks first under the original weights and under the revised weights, respectively?
options: R, then Q
R, then R
P, then Q
Q, then R
P and Q tie, then Q
questions.explanation: Original: P = 3.2 + 2.1 + 1.75 = 7.05; Q = 2.4 + 3.15 + 1.5 = 7.05; R = 2.8 + 2.45 + 2.0 = 7.25, so R leads. Revised: P = 3.2 + 2.7 + 1.05 = 6.95; Q = 2.4 + 4.05 + 0.9 = 7.35; R = 2.8 + 3.15 + 1.2 = 7.15, so Q leads. 'P and Q tie' is true, but only for second place; it traps anyone who stops before computing R.
